title: Few Americans Question Use of Computers in Classroom Lessons November 19, 2025 room-lessons/
author: Larry Cuban
source: Larry Cuban on School Reform and Classroom Practice (larrycuban.wordpress.com),
summary: Larry Cuban builds this post around two paragraphs from Daniel Buck's historical analysis of the digitisation of U.S. public schools, using them to argue that laptops, tablets, and phones have become so deeply normalised in American classrooms that virtually no one -- administrators, teachers, or parents -- still asks whether the devices actually improve learning outcomes. Buck's original argument called on school boards to demand real evidence of efficacy from vendors like Apple, Microsoft, and Google before signing more contracts; Cuban responds that this expectation is naive given how thoroughly one-to-one computing has become an accepted utility, 'the warp-and-woof of daily life,' rather than a product anyone still expects to justify itself with data. Cuban is equally skeptical of Buck's proposed remedy -- returning to shared computer labs and carts to force more judicious use -- noting that today's abundance of devices (one per student, at home and at school) makes any return to artificial scarcity implausible. He ends by noting that whether these devices help, hinder, or are simply neutral to learning remains genuinely unknown heading into 2026, and points readers to Jean Twenge's related New York Times piece on managing devices in schools.
points: Cuban's central claim is that classroom technology has crossed from 'product that must prove itself' to 'accepted utility' -- like electricity or water -- meaning nobody expects vendors to show evidence that devices improve academic outcomes anymore.

He rejects Buck's call for school boards to demand efficacy evidence from tech vendors as a 'trifling' relic of an earlier era, noting that even decades ago companies like Apple, Microsoft, and Google rarely offered such evidence and it was simply assumed.

Buck's proposed fix -- reintroducing computer labs and shared carts to force more deliberate technology use -- is dismissed by Cuban as impractical given the current abundance of devices; scarcity that once forced judicious use no longer exists.

Cuban frames the underlying uncertainty starkly: whether laptops and tablets in classrooms accelerate, confound, or are simply irrelevant to student learning 'is largely unknown, remaining an unanswered question for 2026.'
quotes: Buck believes that U.S. educators should be leery, even skeptical, of using computer devices in lessons, and that teachers and school districts should demand evidence from vendors such as Apple, Microsoft, and Google that their devices and software are “improving academic outcomes.

Note the four "shoulds" in the above paragraph. Yet, the fact of the matter is that the folks who sell computers and software seldom offer proof of effectiveness for the simple reason that they lack "clear evidence of efficacy of their products...." None. Nada. Zip.

These devices have become accepted much like public utilities such as electricity, water, and gas that consumers use daily and pay for monthly. They have become the warp-and-woof of daily life. They have become necessities.

No district administrator, teacher, or parent needs research evidence to justify buying a laptop, tablet, or mobile phone for their schools, classroom, or children just as no research evidence is needed to prove that one must eat to survive.
Today, using laptops and tablets in classroom lessons is as normal as saying the Pledge of Allegiance in the third grade and smelling Lysol in the school’s bathrooms.
Whether they accelerate, confound, or impede student learning, much less academic achievement, is largely unknown, remaining an unanswered question for 2026.
